relevant_findings.topic: Coating type is the primary configuration dimension — NOT quality tier
relevant_findings.finding: Fence coatings follow the same pattern as decks: the primary dimension is coating_type, not quality_tier. Fence coating types: transparent (1-2 year cycle, water repellent + UV filter, wood grain fully visible), semi_transparent (2-4 year cycle, pigmented penetrating stain, wood grain visible through color, PROFESSIONAL STANDARD for wood fences), solid_stain (3-7 year cycle, film-forming, complete grain masking, good for hiding wood defects), paint (5-10 year cycle, film-forming, LEAST RECOMMENDED for wood fences due to moisture-driven peeling). Semi-transparent stain is the professional standard for residential wood fences.

relevant_findings.topic: Paint on wood fences is LEAST RECOMMENDED but not blocked
relevant_findings.finding: Paint on wood fences creates a film that traps moisture migrating through the fence from both sides (fences are fully exposed to weather on both faces). Moisture trapped under paint film causes blistering, peeling, and premature failure — often within 2-3 years on the weather side. Professional recommendation is semi-transparent or solid stain. However, paint cannot be BLOCKED because it is a valid customer choice (color matching to house, HOA requirements). MANDATORY WARNING must be documented when paint is specified on wood fences.

relevant_findings.topic: Fence geometry: (LF x Height) x 2 for both sides
relevant_findings.finding: Fence surface area is calculated as (linear feet x fence height) x 2 to account for BOTH SIDES. Privacy fence: both faces are flat panels — multiply by 2 gives true surface area. Shadowbox: alternating boards on both sides creates 1.5-1.7x the flat surface area per linear foot due to overlapping board edges. Picket: open spacing reduces painted surface to 0.6-0.8x of full panel equivalent. Split rail: component-based (rails only, no panels). CRITICAL: PaintScope provides the FINAL SF after both-sides calculation and style multiplier. The spec does NOT compute geometry.

relevant_findings.topic: Fence style geometric multipliers drive production rate variance
relevant_findings.finding: Fence style is a major production driver because of geometric complexity: Privacy (1.0x) — flat panel, fastest to spray, uniform surface. Shadowbox (1.5-1.7x) — alternating boards on opposite sides create a corrugated profile requiring spray from both sides with angle adjustments to reach recessed faces. Picket (0.6-0.8x surface area but HIGHER per-SF labor) — individual pickets with 4 exposed faces each, gaps between pickets cause overspray waste. Split rail — component-based, rails only (2-3 horizontal rails per section), no panel surface, stain by brush.

relevant_findings.topic: Pressure-treated pine requires 3-6 month seasoning before staining
relevant_findings.finding: New PT lumber is saturated with waterborne preservatives (ACQ, CA-B, MCA) and excess moisture. Wood must season 3-6 months before staining to allow preservative cure and MC to drop below 19%. Staining green PT wood results in poor penetration, blotchy appearance, and premature failure. HARD STOP if wood age < 3 months. Water bead test (sprinkle water — if it beads, wood is not ready; if it absorbs within 30 seconds, wood is ready) is the field-expedient verification method.

Cedar fences contain water-soluble extractive tannins that bleed through coatings, causing dark brown/red discoloration. Tannin bleed is most severe with water-based coatings and at end-grain (top of fence boards). For penetrating stains (transparent, semi-transparent), some tannin bleed is aesthetically acceptable. For solid stain or paint, tannin-blocking primer is REQUIRED on cedar to prevent bleed-through. Oil-based stains resist tannin bleed better than water-based on cedar substrates.

relevant_findings.topic: Back-brushing mandatory when spraying penetrating stains on fences
relevant_findings.finding: Spray application of penetrating stains on fences REQUIRES back-brushing. Spray deposits stain on the surface but does not force it into wood pores. Back-brushing with a stiff synthetic bristle brush works stain into the wood grain, ensuring proper penetration and even absorption. This is the same mandate as deck staining. On fences, back-brushing also helps work stain into board-to-board joints and end-grain at the top of boards. Spray-only application of penetrating stains is NOT acceptable.

Fence spray application generates 15-30% material waste beyond theoretical coverage. Sources: overspray through picket gaps (highest waste — up to 30%), overspray past fence ends and top, wind drift (fences are fully exposed outdoor structures with no containment), board edge and end-grain over-absorption. Privacy fences are at the lower end (15-20%) because the solid panel catches most spray. Picket fences are at the upper end (25-30%) because gaps allow spray-through. Material estimates must include waste factor.

Fences must be stained/painted on BOTH sides, which creates unique access and sequencing challenges. Typical approach: (1) Set up protection on one side, spray that face, back-brush. (2) Move equipment to opposite side, set up protection, spray second face, back-brush. For privacy fences, crew can only access one face at a time — the other face is the neighbor's side, requiring access coordination. For shadowbox, both sides must be sprayed at angles to reach recessed boards. Split rail is accessible from both sides simultaneously.

relevant_findings.topic: Wood fence scope limitation for v1 — metal, composite, vinyl deferred
relevant_findings.finding: This v1 spec focuses exclusively on WOOD fences (cedar, PT pine). Metal fences (wrought iron, aluminum, chain link) route to SF_METAL_EXT_v1 — different substrate, primer system, and coating chemistry entirely. Composite fences are maintenance-free by design (similar to composite decking). Vinyl fences are rarely painted. Both composite and vinyl are edge cases noted but not built with full task paths in v1.

Weathered wood fences (UV-degraded, grayed, loose fiber) follow a similar chemical restoration protocol to decks but with VERTICAL surface considerations: (1) Alkaline strip/cleaner — removes failed coating residue, mildew, dirt. (2) Acid brightener — oxalic acid for cedar tannin, citric acid alternative. (3) Rinse and dry. Vertical fences drain better than horizontal decks (less moisture retention), so dry time is shorter (12-24 hours vs 24-48 hours for decks). Chemical runoff onto landscaping below fence requires protection.

relevant_findings.topic: Post and cap treatment as included scope
relevant_findings.finding: Fence posts (4x4 or 6x6) and post caps are part of the fence system and included in this spec. Posts are typically the same substrate as fence boards but have exposed end-grain at the top that absorbs stain at 2-3x the face rate. Post caps (wood, copper, or composite) may require different treatment — copper caps are not painted, composite caps may not accept stain. Wood post caps are stained with the fence. Post count is derived from fence LF (typically one post per 6-8 LF section).

condition_drivers.impact: PRIMARY CONFIGURATION DIMENSION. Drives coating chemistry (penetrating vs film-forming), maintenance cycle, failure mode profile, primer requirement (none for penetrating, tannin-block for solid/paint on cedar), material coverage rates, and UV protection level. Paint is LEAST RECOMMENDED for wood fences — triggers mandatory risk warning. Replaces quality_tier as the primary dimension for this spec.
condition_drivers.notes: Semi-transparent is the professional standard default. Paint triggers RC-007 warning. No semi-solid category for fences (unlike decks) — the jump from semi-transparent to solid is more common on vertical fence surfaces.

condition_drivers.impact: Drives prep module selection. New: seasoning verification (PT pine) + mill glaze consideration. Weathered: chemical restoration protocol (strip, brighten, rinse). Previously_coated: assess existing coating integrity — clean and recoat if sound, strip if failing. Each condition has fundamentally different prep time and materials.
condition_drivers.notes: This spec covers BOTH new and existing fences. Wood_condition dimension handles prep module selection. RC-001.

condition_drivers.impact: Drives geometric multiplier applied to base (LF x Height x 2) calculation AND production rate. Privacy (1.0x, fastest spray). Shadowbox (1.5-1.7x surface area, angle spray required). Picket (0.6-0.8x surface area but higher per-SF labor, highest overspray waste). Split rail (component-based, brush-only, no panel surface). PaintScope applies style multiplier BEFORE delivering final SF to spec.
condition_drivers.notes: Privacy is ~70% of residential fences. Shadowbox is the most labor-intensive per LF due to corrugated profile requiring angle spray from both sides.

condition_drivers.impact: Drives prep chemistry and primer requirements. Cedar: tannin bleed management (oxalic acid brightener), oil-based stain preferred, tannin-blocking primer required for solid stain/paint. PT pine: 3-6 month seasoning requirement (HARD STOP if < 3 months), MC < 19% verification, no tannin concern. Composite and vinyl EXCLUDED per RC-004.
condition_drivers.notes: PT pine is ~65% of residential fences (cost-driven). Cedar is ~30% (premium aesthetic). Redwood is rare for fences in most markets — grouped with cedar for tannin management.

condition_drivers.impact: Spray_backbrush is the production method for privacy and shadowbox fences (fastest for large panel areas). Brush is primary for split rail and detail/touchup. Roll can be used on privacy fence flat panels but has lower production rate than spray. IMPORTANT: spray on fence with penetrating stains = ALWAYS add back-brush. 15-30% spray waste factor applies.
condition_drivers.notes: Spray_backbrush is the fence equivalent of deck spray_backbrush. Two-person crew: one sprays, one back-brushes. Brush-only for split rail.

quality_differences.description: Economy/minimal protection. Water repellent with UV filter — no color pigment. Wood grain and natural color fully visible. 1-2 year maintenance cycle (annual recoat typical). Fastest to apply. Lowest material cost. No color matching. Best for new cedar where natural wood appearance is desired.
quality_differences.typical_use: New cedar fences where homeowner wants natural wood look. Annual maintenance commitment required. Not recommended for PT pine (greenish chemical color shows through).

quality_differences.description: PROFESSIONAL STANDARD for wood fences. Pigmented penetrating stain — wood grain visible through color. UV protection from pigment load. 2-4 year maintenance cycle. Good balance of aesthetics, protection, and maintainability. Easy maintenance recoat (clean and recoat, no stripping). Hides PT pine green tint while showing wood texture.
quality_differences.typical_use: Standard residential fence staining. Most contractor-recommended option. ~55% of professional fence staining work. Works well on both cedar and PT pine.

quality_differences.description: Film-forming coating. Complete grain masking — opaque color. 3-7 year cycle. Better longevity than penetrating stains on vertical surfaces (no foot traffic wear). Good for hiding wood defects, knots, color inconsistency, or previous stain color. Requires more prep for recoat (sand, possibly strip if failing). Tannin-blocking primer required on cedar.
quality_differences.typical_use: Color matching to house. Covering weathered or stained wood. HOA color requirements. Homeowners wanting longest maintenance cycle. ~30% of professional fence work.

quality_differences.description: Full film-forming paint system. Primer + topcoat. 5-10 year cycle on vertical surfaces BUT highest failure risk on wood fences. Moisture migrates through fence from both sides — trapped under paint film, causes blistering and peeling. LEAST RECOMMENDED for wood fences. MANDATORY WARNING when specified. Requires full prime-paint pipeline.
quality_differences.typical_use: HOA mandated white fences. Customer insists on specific paint color. Understand that failure rate is highest of all options. ~10% of fence work. Document risk.

failure_modes.name: Moisture-driven peeling on painted wood fences
failure_modes.description: Paint forms a film on both fence faces that traps moisture migrating through wood from rain exposure on either side. Unlike a wall (one side protected from weather), a fence is exposed on BOTH sides. Moisture enters from the weather side, migrates through wood, and becomes trapped under paint on the lee side. This causes blistering, bubbling, and sheet peeling — often within 2-3 years. The weather-exposed face fails first.
failure_modes.prevention: Use penetrating stains (transparent or semi-transparent) instead of paint on wood fences. If paint is specified, document risk warning. Use premium 100% acrylic exterior paint with high permeability rating. Ensure wood MC < 19% before painting. Back-prime all boards (both faces) before assembly if possible.
failure_modes.detection: Blistering or bubbling of paint film. Peeling sheets of paint, typically on the weather-facing side first. Soft, damp wood under lifted paint film.

failure_modes.name: Premature stain failure on unseasoned PT pine
failure_modes.description: Stain applied to new PT pine that has not seasoned (< 3 months since treatment) fails to penetrate properly. Waterborne preservatives and excess moisture in the wood repel stain. Result: blotchy, uneven appearance within weeks, complete stain failure within first season. This is the most common fence staining callback.
failure_modes.prevention: HARD STOP: verify PT pine seasoning age >= 3 months (6 months preferred). Perform water bead test — water must absorb within 30 seconds. Verify MC < 19%. If wood is too new, schedule staining for later date. Do not apply stain to green PT wood under any circumstances.
failure_modes.detection: Blotchy, uneven stain absorption pattern. Stain sitting on surface rather than penetrating. Rapid color loss within first season. Water beading on stained surface (stain not penetrated).

failure_modes.name: Cedar tannin bleed-through
failure_modes.description: Water-soluble extractive tannins in cedar bleed through solid stain and paint coatings, causing dark brown/red discoloration streaks. Most severe with water-based coatings and at end-grain locations (top of fence boards). Tannin bleed stains adjacent surfaces (concrete walkways, driveways) when washed by rain.
failure_modes.prevention: For penetrating stains: accept some tannin bleed as natural (aesthetically compatible). For solid stain/paint: use tannin-blocking primer (shellac-based or specialty exterior tannin block). Consider oil-based stain for better tannin resistance. Treat with oxalic acid brightener before coating to dissolve surface tannins.
failure_modes.detection: Dark brown/reddish streaks through solid stain or paint coating. Discoloration concentrated at end-grain (board tops) and knot areas. Staining of adjacent concrete or walkways below fence.

failure_modes.name: Overstaining — excessive product buildup
failure_modes.description: Applying too much penetrating stain creates a thick surface film on what should be an absorbed-into-wood finish. Common when back-brushing is skipped (spray pooling in board joints and bottom edges) or when recoating over still-wet first coat. The excess stain forms a sticky, tacky film that does not cure properly, attracts dirt, and peels.
failure_modes.prevention: Apply thin coats. Back-brush thoroughly to work stain into wood and remove excess from surface. Do not allow pooling at board joints, bottom edges, or horizontal rails. Allow first coat to absorb before second coat application. Wipe excess stain from non-absorbing surfaces (fastener heads, hardware).
failure_modes.detection: Sticky, tacky surface that does not cure. Shiny, film-like appearance on what should be a matte penetrating finish. Dirt adhesion to tacky surface. Peeling of thick stain film at board joints.

failure_modes.name: UV degradation and graying on unprotected or transparent-coated wood
failure_modes.description: Unprotected wood or transparent-coated fence surfaces undergo rapid UV photodegradation of lignin. The natural wood binder breaks down, leaving silvery-gray cellulose fibers. Transparent coatings with UV filters slow but do not stop this process — annual recoat is required. South and west-facing fence sections degrade fastest due to maximum UV exposure.
failure_modes.prevention: Use semi-transparent or higher pigment stain for longer UV protection. Transparent coatings require annual maintenance cycle. Educate customer on maintenance expectations by coating type. South/west-facing sections may need more frequent maintenance than north/east-facing.
failure_modes.detection: Silvery-gray color replacing natural wood tone. Loose surface fibers. Rough texture when rubbed. Color loss concentrated on sun-exposed faces.

notes_for_materials_manager: This is primarily a STAIN spec (like deck). Primary materials are penetrating stains, not paints. Material system branches by coating_type: transparent, semi_transparent, solid_stain, paint.

Penetrating stains (transparent, semi-transparent) do NOT use primer. Primer seals wood surface and prevents stain penetration. Only solid stain and paint on cedar require tannin-blocking primer. Paint on any wood fence substrate requires standard exterior primer.

Coverage rates for fences — penetrating stain: 200-300 SF/gal on smooth new wood, 150-250 SF/gal on rough/weathered wood. Solid stain: 300-400 SF/gal (film-forming). Paint: 350-400 SF/gal. End-grain (top of fence boards) absorbs 2-3x normal rate.
15-30% spray waste factor must be included in material quantity calculations. Privacy fence: 15-20% waste. Shadowbox: 20-25% waste. Picket: 25-30% waste (highest due to spray-through gaps).

Cedar tannin management materials: oxalic acid brightener (powder, mix on-site) for pre-stain tannin treatment. Tannin-blocking primer (shellac-based) for solid stain/paint on cedar. Oil-based stain products preferred for cedar (better tannin resistance than water-based).
Weathered wood prep materials: sodium percarbonate deck/fence cleaner (alkaline strip), oxalic acid or citric acid brightener (acid step). Same chemistry as deck restoration.
Back-brushing supplies: stiff synthetic bristle brush, 4-6 inch for panel faces, 2-3 inch for posts and detail. Replace frequently — stain degrades bristles.
Masking materials: plastic sheeting (4-6 mil) for landscaping/hardscape protection during spray. Minimal taping — fences have few hard-line masking interfaces (unlike siding-to-trim).

Paint option (least recommended): exterior acrylic latex primer + exterior acrylic latex topcoat. High-permeability (breathable) formulation critical for fence application to allow moisture vapor transmission.
notes_for_sop_librarian: Module structure: setup → protect → clean/strip → prep → stain_apply (or prime → paint_apply for paint option) → cleanup → teardown. NO prime module for penetrating stains (transparent, semi-transparent). Prime module only for solid stain on cedar or paint option.
Seasoning verification task is FIRST for new PT pine — verify 3-6 month age and MC < 19%. HARD STOP if wood is < 3 months old. Water bead test as field verification.

Both-sides workflow: each face is a separate pass. (1) Protect side A landscaping/hardscape. (2) Spray + back-brush side A. (3) Move equipment. (4) Protect side B landscaping/hardscape. (5) Spray + back-brush side B. Neighbor coordination may be required for side B access.

Fence style affects SOP: Privacy — straightforward flat panel spray per face. Shadowbox — angle spray required from both sides to reach recessed board faces. Picket — spray from one side, catch overspray on back side, then touch up second side. Split rail — brush-only, no spray, 2-3 rails per section + posts.

Back-brushing is MANDATORY when spraying penetrating stains. Spray deposits stain on surface; back-brushing forces stain into wood grain. Same mandate as deck spec. Two-person crew: one sprays, one follows immediately with stiff bristle brush.

Weathered wood chemical restoration is a conditional module: (1) alkaline strip/clean, (2) acid brighten, (3) rinse. Vertical fences drain well — 12-24 hour dry time before staining (shorter than deck's 24-48 hours). Chemical runoff onto landscaping requires protection below fence line.
Post end-grain treatment: tops of fence posts absorb stain at 2-3x face rate. Apply extra stain to post tops and top edges of fence boards. Dedicated pass for end-grain after face staining.

Paint option SOP: prime all surfaces (both faces), dry, topcoat both faces. Two coats recommended. Full prime-paint pipeline with standard exterior paint SOP. Document moisture-peeling risk warning in project record.
Solid stain on cedar SOP: apply tannin-blocking primer to both faces first, dry, then apply solid stain both faces. Primer is NOT optional on cedar with solid stain.

Environmental SOP: stain when surface temp 50-90F. Avoid direct sun during application (flash drying). Wind < 10 mph for spray. Fences are fully exposed structures — wind drift is a primary overspray concern.
notes_for_estimation_engineer: Production rates — Spray stain privacy fence: 215 SF/hr (per face, one side at a time). Brush/roll stain: 120 SF/hr. These rates include back-brushing for penetrating stains.
Spray stain picket fence: 200 LF/hr (per face). Spray stain privacy fence: 100 LF/hr (per face). These are LF-based rates accounting for fence height and both-sides in the LF measurement.
Shadowbox fence spray stain: ~150 SF/hr per face (slower than privacy due to angle spray and recessed board access). Approximately 70% of privacy fence rate.
Split rail fence: brush stain 40-60 LF/hr (per rail, 2-3 rails per section). Component-based — each rail is a linear element. Posts at 15-20 min per post.
Post staining: included in fence LF rate for panel fences (posts are stained as part of the panel pass). Split rail posts are separate at 15-20 min per post (4 faces + end-grain top).
Weathered wood chemical restoration: 80-120 SF/hr for full 3-step process. 12-24 hour dry time after — may require separate mobilization day.
Fence geometry: PaintScope delivers FINAL SF after (LF x Height x 2) calculation and fence_style multiplier. Spec receives SF and applies rate. Spec does NOT compute geometry. RC-006.

Both-sides labor: production rates are per-face. Total project labor = rate x SF for side A + rate x SF for side B + equipment move time between sides (~0.5-1.0 hr per mobilization move). PaintScope's final SF already accounts for both sides.
Material waste factors: privacy 15-20%, shadowbox 20-25%, picket 25-30%. Include in material quantity calculation, NOT in labor rate.
Environmental conditions EXCLUDED from estimation — SOP/process concerns, not estimatable at bid time. Per established exterior spec convention. RC-002.
No height modifier for standard fences — typical residential fence height is 4-6 ft, all work performed from ground level. No ladder, scaffold, or lift scenarios for standard fence staining.
Paint option rates: primer spray 250-350 SF/hr, paint spray_backroll 200-300 SF/hr. Film-forming application, different from penetrating stain rates.

assumptions.value: Wood fence staining/painting — privacy, shadowbox, picket, split rail styles. Covers new construction AND existing/maintenance. Exterior vertical wood surfaces. Wood substrates only (cedar, PT pine).
assumptions.note: This spec covers BOTH NC and existing fences. Wood_condition dimension handles new vs weathered vs previously_coated. Metal fences route to SF_METAL_EXT_v1. Composite and vinyl are edge cases excluded from v1.

assumptions.value: coating_type is the primary configuration dimension. No traditional QT2-QT5 quality tier dimension.
assumptions.source: Researcher analysis; RC-003; sibling deck spec pattern
assumptions.note: Fence coating selection maps loosely to quality: transparent = economy, semi_transparent = standard, solid_stain = enhanced, paint = premium longevity but highest risk. Coating_type drives fundamentally different chemistry and failure profiles.

assumptions.value: Metal fences route to SF_METAL_EXT_v1. Composite and vinyl fences excluded from v1.
assumptions.note: Metal fences have entirely different substrate, primer, and coating chemistry. Composite is maintenance-free. Vinyl is rarely painted. None are wood fence scope.

assumptions.value: Mandatory back-brushing on all spray-applied penetrating stains. No spray-only option for penetrating stains on fences.
assumptions.source: Exterior_Fences_Doctrine.md; RC-005; sibling deck spec pattern
assumptions.note: Same mandate as deck spec. Brush forces stain into wood grain pores. Spray deposits on surface only.

assumptions.value: PaintScope provides final SF after (LF x Height x 2) and style multiplier. Spec does NOT compute geometry.
assumptions.note: Fence geometry calculation is a PaintScope responsibility. Spec receives the computed SF and applies production rates.

assumptions.value: Paint on wood fences is LEAST RECOMMENDED but not blocked. Mandatory risk warning when specified.
assumptions.note: Customer choice. HOA requirements may mandate paint. Document peeling risk.

uncertainties.detail: Doctrine provides 1.5-1.7x range for shadowbox fences. The exact multiplier depends on board width, gap width, and overlap depth — which vary by builder and region. A single fixed multiplier may under- or over-estimate by 10-15%.
uncertainties.recommendation: Use 1.6x as default. PaintScope should allow override for specific shadowbox configurations. Flag for field calibration.

uncertainties.detail: Split rail fences are component-based (rails + posts, no panels) and do not fit the SF-based rate model used for other fence styles. Production is better modeled as LF per rail or EA per post. Doctrine provides limited rate guidance for split rail.
uncertainties.recommendation: Model split rail as separate line items: LF per rail (2-3 rails per section) + EA per post. Flag for field calibration of rates.

uncertainties.detail: Both-sides staining requires access to the neighbor's side of the fence. Access coordination (negotiation, gate access, moving neighbor's items) is not captured in production rates but can add 0.5-2 hours to a project.
uncertainties.recommendation: Note as project-level overhead. Not a per-SF rate adjustment. Estimator should assess access during site visit.

uncertainties.topic: PT pine moisture content threshold: 15% vs 19%
uncertainties.detail: Deck doctrine specifies MC < 15% for stain application. Fence doctrine indicates MC < 19% for PT pine (higher threshold because vertical surfaces do not pool water). The difference reflects the reduced moisture failure risk on vertical vs horizontal surfaces. Using 15% for fences may unnecessarily delay projects.
uncertainties.recommendation: Use MC < 19% for fence PT pine (vertical surface tolerance). MC < 15% remains the standard for horizontal deck surfaces. Flag for doctrine reconciliation if needed.

zones.upgrade_scenario: Upgrades to full_cover when application_method = spray_backbrush
zones.notes: Landscaping, mulch beds, and ground cover along fence base on both sides. Drop cloth/plastic along fence line. Primary overspray and drip zone.

zones.upgrade_scenario: Upgrades to full_cover when application_method = spray_backbrush
zones.notes: Walkways, driveways, patios running along fence line. Drop cloth runners or plastic sheeting along fence base. Stain overspray on concrete is difficult to remove.

zones.condition: when fence ties into house siding
zones.upgrade_scenario: Upgrades to full_cover when application_method = spray_backbrush
zones.notes: House siding where fence attaches to structure. Tape and plastic at fence-to-house junction. Fence often ties into house at garage or side yard.

zones.condition: when vehicles parked near fence (driveway fences)
zones.notes: Vehicles parked near fence being sprayed. Overspray drift onto vehicles is a liability risk. Full cover with plastic sheeting or relocate vehicles. Always spray away from vehicles when possible.

zones.condition: when spraying fence side facing neighbor
zones.notes: Neighbor's landscaping, structures, and items near fence. Drop cloth along neighbor's side of fence base. Coordinate with neighbor. Wind drift is primary concern.

protection_zones_analysis.cross_spec_protection_note: Fence-to-house siding junction protection is this spec's responsibility. Gate hardware masking is included in this spec. Adjacent structure protection (neighbor's shed, garage, etc.) is this spec's responsibility if within overspray range.

adjacent_surfaces.notes: House siding where fence ties into structure. Different product systems (stain vs paint). Protection required at junction. No cut-in — fence stain terminates at house wall with gap or trim board.
Fence posts are integral to fence system. Same stain product. Stained as part of fence pass. Posts have end-grain tops requiring extra stain application.
Gates within fence line. Same stain product. Stained as part of fence but gate hardware requires masking. Gate may need to be stained in open position for access to both faces.
Walkways and driveways adjacent to fence at grade. Not in scope — protection only. Stain drips and overspray on concrete are difficult to remove.
Ground/landscaping at fence base. Not in scope — protection only. Both sides of fence have ground-level protection needs.

adjacency_analysis.key_finding: Fence field has NO edge work within this spec. The fence-to-house junction is a protection-only relationship (different product systems). Posts and gates are integral components stained with the same product. All ground-level adjacencies are protection-only.

values.mc_above_19_percent: HARD STOP — do not stain PT pine
values.mc_above_15_percent: HARD STOP — do not stain cedar

affected_conditions.notes: MC > 19% (PT pine) or > 15% (cedar) prevents proper stain penetration. Hard stop. Reschedule. Water bead test as field-expedient verification.

values.neighbor_access_required: coordinate access to neighbor's side of fence

affected_conditions.notes: Fence staining requires both-sides access. Neighbor coordination is a project-level scheduling concern. May require separate mobilization for each side if access is restricted.

excluded_conditions.rationale: Environmental conditions are important to the staining PROCESS but are NOT estimatable. They are unpredictable, change daily, and cannot be set as fixed conditions for an estimate. Per established exterior spec convention. RC-002.

excluded.reason: Unpredictable. Changes hourly. Fences are fully exposed — wind drift is primary overspray concern but not estimatable.
Varies by time of day, sun angle, season. Not predictable at bid time.
Weather-dependent. Not predictable at bid time.
Direct sun causes flash drying of stain. Scheduling concern, not estimation.

valid_input_states.rationale: Three input states correspond to the three wood_condition values. SS_EXT_BARE_WOOD = new wood (PT pine, cedar) awaiting first coat. SS_EXT_STAINED = previously stained fence with existing coating (sound or failing). SS_EXT_WEATHERED = UV-degraded, grayed wood with lost or eroded coating requiring chemical restoration.

output_state.rationale: Transparent and semi-transparent produce SS_EXT_STAINED. Solid stain produces SS_EXT_STAINED_SOLID. Paint produces SS_EXT_PAINTED. Output state determines maintenance recoat approach — penetrating stains are clean-and-recoat, solid/paint require sand-and-recoat.

adjacent_state_protection_analysis.rationale: Stain overspray on finished siding is difficult to remove (penetrating product absorbs into paint). Full cover when siding is finished. Light mask when unfinished because stain discolors bare wood differently than intended siding finish.
Penetrating stain on concrete is extremely difficult to remove — absorbs into pores. Full cover for any hardscape adjacent to fence spray zone.

exterior_substrate_states.description: New, uncoated wood fence. Pressure-treated pine or cedar. May have mill glaze from sawmill planing. PT pine requires 3-6 month seasoning before staining.
exterior_substrate_states.prep_requirements: Verify seasoning (PT pine: 3-6 months, HARD STOP if < 3 months). Moisture test (MC < 19% for PT pine, MC < 15% for cedar). Mill glaze consideration (less common on fence boards than deck boards — rough-sawn fence boards typically do not have mill glaze). Water absorption test to verify readiness.
exterior_substrate_states.primer_type: None for penetrating stains. Tannin-blocking primer for solid stain/paint on cedar. Standard exterior primer for paint on PT pine.
exterior_substrate_states.notes: New fence construction. PT pine is ~65% of residential fences. Cedar ~30%.

exterior_substrate_states.description: Previously stained wood fence with existing penetrating or film-forming coating. Coating may be sound (maintenance recoat) or failing (requires strip/sand).
exterior_substrate_states.prep_requirements: Assess existing coating integrity. Sound penetrating stain: clean (power wash low-pressure) and recoat directly. Failed penetrating stain: light sand, clean, recoat. Sound solid stain: light sand for adhesion, recoat. Failed solid stain/paint: full strip to bare wood, then treat as weathered.
exterior_substrate_states.primer_type: None for penetrating stain recoat. Solid stain/paint over different product type may require adhesion primer.
exterior_substrate_states.notes: Previously coated condition. Prep varies by existing coating type and condition.

exterior_substrate_states.description: UV-degraded, grayed wood fence with lost or severely eroded coating. Loose wood fibers, silvery-gray color from lignin photodegradation. May have mildew growth.
exterior_substrate_states.prep_requirements: Chemical restoration protocol: (1) alkaline strip/clean, (2) acid brighten (oxalic acid for cedar), (3) rinse. Allow 12-24 hours drying (shorter than deck due to vertical drainage). Verify MC after drying. May require light sanding to remove remaining loose fibers.
exterior_substrate_states.primer_type: None for penetrating stains applied to restored bare wood.
exterior_substrate_states.notes: Weathered condition. Most labor-intensive prep. Chemical restoration 12-24 hour dry time before staining.

exterior_access_type_analysis.treatment: No height modifier for standard residential fences. Fence height 4-6 ft — all work performed from ground level. No ladder, scaffold, or lift scenarios.

scenarios.notes: Standard residential fence. All staining performed from ground level. Crew walks along fence line. This is the only access scenario for residential fences.

exterior_access_type_analysis.key_distinction: Unlike siding or masonry specs, fence work is always ground-level. Standard residential fences are 4-6 ft tall — well within standing reach. Tall privacy fences (8 ft) may require step stool for top edge but this is negligible. No FAC_EXT_ACCESS modifier applies.

exterior_environmental_constraints.note: Environmental constraints are documented here for SOP reference but are EXCLUDED from estimation modifiers per established exterior spec convention. RC-002.

sop_reference_only.note: Fences are fully exposed outdoor structures — wind drift is the PRIMARY overspray concern. Higher sensitivity to wind than wall painting because no building mass to block wind.
Below 50: stain won't penetrate properly, slow cure. Above 90: flash drying, uneven absorption.

sop_reference_only.rule: Surface temp must be >= 5F above dew point
sop_reference_only.note: Morning dew on fence surfaces — wait until dry.

sop_reference_only.rule: Wood MC < 19% for PT pine, < 15% for cedar (hard stop)
sop_reference_only.note: Water bead test as field verification. Pin-type moisture meter authoritative.

sop_reference_only.rule: Avoid staining in direct sun — causes flash drying and uneven absorption
sop_reference_only.note: Schedule shaded side first. Work follows shade pattern throughout day.

sop_reference_only.rule: No stain application if rain within 24 hours
sop_reference_only.note: Penetrating stains need dry time to cure in wood fibers. Rain washes uncured stain from surface.

sop_reference_only.rule: PT pine: minimum 3 months seasoning (HARD STOP). 6 months preferred.
sop_reference_only.note: Project-level gate. Verify with builder/GC for new construction.

privacy_stain_spray_backbrush.notes: Spray + back-brush on privacy fence flat panel. Per face (one side at a time). 2-person crew. Includes back-brushing time.

privacy_stain_brush_roll.notes: Brush or roller application on privacy fence. Per face. Slower but lower waste (no overspray).

privacy_stain_spray_lf.notes: Privacy fence spray stain in LF terms (accounts for 6 ft height x both sides). Per the brief's LF-based rate.

picket_stain_spray_lf.notes: Picket fence spray stain in LF terms. Faster LF rate because less surface area per LF (gaps between pickets). Higher material waste (25-30%).

shadowbox_stain_spray_backbrush.notes: Shadowbox fence spray + back-brush. ~70% of privacy rate due to corrugated profile and angle spray requirement.

split_rail_stain_brush.notes: Split rail fence brush stain per rail. 2-3 rails per section. No panel surface — rails only.

split_rail_post_stain.notes: Per post for split rail. 4 faces + end-grain top. Brush application.

fence_sanding.notes: Fence board sanding for prep. Same rate as deck floor sanding.

chemical_restoration_full.notes: Full 3-step weathered wood restoration (strip + brighten + rinse). 12-24 hr dry time after.

power_wash_existing.notes: Low-pressure wash for previously coated or dirty fence. Fan tip, 1200-1500 PSI max.

equipment_move_between_sides.notes: Time to move spray equipment, hoses, protection materials from one side of fence to the other. One move per project.

gate_hardware_masking.notes: Mask gate hinges, latches, locks before staining. Per gate unit.

key_decisions.decision: This spec uses coating_type as primary dimension instead of quality_tier. Coating types: transparent, semi_transparent, solid_stain, paint. Paint is included but flagged as LEAST RECOMMENDED.
key_decisions.rationale: Fence coating selection drives fundamentally different chemistry (penetrating vs film-forming), failure modes, maintenance cycles, and primer requirements. Paint is valid but high-risk for wood fences. RC-003, RC-007.

key_decisions.topic: NC and existing fences in one spec
key_decisions.decision: This spec covers all wood conditions: new, weathered, previously_coated. Not NC-only.
key_decisions.rationale: Wood_condition dimension handles prep module selection. The core staining workflow is the same — only prep differs. Same pattern as deck sibling. RC-001.

key_decisions.decision: One primary paintable item: ITM_EXT_FENCE_FIELD (SF). Posts and gates are included in the fence field scope (not separate line items). Split rail rails are modeled within the fence field using LF-based rates.
key_decisions.rationale: Unlike decks (which have 4 distinct items with different UOM and rates), fences are primarily measured as total surface area. Posts are stained as part of the panel pass. Gates are small and included. Fence style multiplier accounts for geometric complexity. Simpler item model than deck.

key_decisions.decision: Metal fences excluded (route to SF_METAL_EXT_v1). Composite and vinyl excluded. Cedar and PT pine are the primary substrates.
key_decisions.rationale: Metal, composite, and vinyl fences have entirely different coating systems. Wood fences are the primary professional painting contractor scope. RC-004.

key_decisions.topic: Spray always includes back-brush for penetrating stains
key_decisions.decision: Application method 'spray_backbrush' is a single unit for penetrating stains. No spray-only option for penetrating stains.
key_decisions.rationale: Same mandate as deck spec. Spray deposits on surface; back-brushing forces stain into wood pores. RC-005.

key_decisions.topic: Geometry computed by PaintScope, not spec
key_decisions.decision: PaintScope provides final SF after (LF x Height x 2) calculation and fence_style multiplier. Spec receives SF and applies production rate.
key_decisions.rationale: Fence geometry calculation involves fence_style multipliers that are PaintScope's responsibility. Spec should not duplicate geometry logic. RC-006.

key_decisions.topic: Paint option triggers mandatory risk warning
key_decisions.decision: Paint on wood fences is LEAST RECOMMENDED. When paint coating_type is selected, MANDATORY risk documentation in project record.
key_decisions.rationale: Moisture-driven peeling is the #1 paint failure mode on wood fences. Both-sides weather exposure makes fences the worst substrate for paint film. Customer choice is respected but risk is documented. RC-007.

key_decisions.decision: No FAC_EXT_ACCESS height modifier for residential fences. All work is ground-level.
key_decisions.rationale: Standard residential fences are 4-6 ft tall. All staining is performed from standing position at ground level. No ladder, scaffold, or lift scenarios.

key_decisions.decision: EXCLUDED from estimation modifiers. Per established exterior spec convention.
key_decisions.rationale: Environmental conditions are unpredictable at bid time. SOP/process concerns only. RC-002.

key_decisions.topic: Both-sides workflow as single project scope
key_decisions.decision: Both fence faces are included in project scope. PaintScope SF includes both sides. Equipment move between sides is a fixed overhead item.
key_decisions.rationale: A fence staining project inherently includes both sides. The (LF x Height x 2) geometry and equipment move time capture the both-sides scope.

key_decisions.decision: Penetrating stains (transparent, semi-transparent) have NO prime module. Stain applies directly to prepared wood. Solid stain on cedar requires tannin-blocking primer. Paint option requires full primer.
key_decisions.rationale: Primer seals wood surface and prevents stain penetration. Same pattern as deck sibling. Primer only enters the pipeline for film-forming coatings on cedar or for the paint option.

key_decisions.decision: fence_style dimension: privacy, shadowbox, picket, split_rail. Drives geometric multiplier AND production rate selection.
key_decisions.rationale: Each fence style has dramatically different surface area per LF and production characteristics. Privacy is the baseline (1.0x). PaintScope applies the style multiplier to deliver final SF.

proposed_new_keys.rationale: Primary configuration dimension for fence spec. Drives coating chemistry, primer requirement, failure mode profile, and maintenance cycle.
proposed_new_keys.notes: Project-level setting. Replaces quality_tier as the primary dimension. Paint included but flagged as LEAST RECOMMENDED.

proposed_new_keys.rationale: Drives prep module selection. Each condition has fundamentally different prep time and materials.
proposed_new_keys.notes: Project-level setting. Determines which prep tasks are activated.

proposed_new_keys.rationale: Drives geometric multiplier (PaintScope applies to final SF) and production rate selection. Each style has dramatically different labor characteristics.
proposed_new_keys.notes: Project-level setting. PaintScope uses this to compute final SF from base (LF x Height x 2).

proposed_new_keys.rationale: Drives prep chemistry (tannin management for cedar, seasoning for PT pine) and primer requirements.
proposed_new_keys.notes: Project-level setting. PT pine ~65%, cedar ~30% of residential fences.

proposed_new_keys.rationale: Count of gates in fence line. Each gate requires hardware masking (hinges, latches, locks). Gates may need open-position staining for both-face access.
proposed_new_keys.notes: Gate count for masking task estimation.

research_corrections.original_assumption: Spec covers new construction only (NC pattern from sibling specs)
research_corrections.corrected_to: Spec covers BOTH NC and existing fences. Wood_condition dimension handles new vs weathered vs previously_coated.
research_corrections.rationale: Same pattern as deck sibling. The spec name is SF_FENCE_EXT_v1 (no NC in name). Fence staining uses the same products on all wood conditions — only prep differs.

research_corrections.original_assumption: Environmental conditions might be estimatable for outdoor fences
research_corrections.corrected_to: Environmental conditions EXCLUDED from estimation per established exterior spec convention.
research_corrections.rationale: Same convention as deck, masonry, and siding siblings. Environmental conditions are unpredictable at bid time.

research_corrections.original_assumption: Standard QT2-QT5 quality tier dimension applies
research_corrections.corrected_to: coating_type is the primary configuration dimension. No traditional quality tier.
research_corrections.rationale: Same pattern as deck sibling. Coating type drives fundamentally different chemistry, failure modes, and maintenance expectations.

research_corrections.original_assumption: All fence substrate types (metal, composite, vinyl) included
research_corrections.corrected_to: WOOD ONLY for v1. Metal fences route to SF_METAL_EXT_v1. Composite and vinyl excluded.
research_corrections.rationale: Metal, composite, and vinyl fences have entirely different coating systems and are not standard painting contractor scope for wood staining.

research_corrections.original_assumption: Spray-only application is acceptable for fences
research_corrections.corrected_to: Back-brushing MANDATORY when spraying penetrating stains. Same mandate as deck.
research_corrections.rationale: Spray deposits on surface only. Back-brushing forces stain into wood pores for proper penetration.

research_corrections.original_assumption: Spec computes fence geometry from LF input
research_corrections.corrected_to: PaintScope provides FINAL SF after (LF x Height x 2) and style multiplier. Spec does NOT compute geometry.
research_corrections.rationale: Geometry calculation is PaintScope's responsibility. Spec receives computed SF.

research_corrections.original_assumption: Paint might be excluded from fence spec
research_corrections.corrected_to: Paint is included as a coating_type option but flagged as LEAST RECOMMENDED with mandatory risk warning.
research_corrections.rationale: Paint is a valid customer choice (HOA requirements, color matching) but has the highest failure rate on wood fences due to moisture-driven peeling.
